# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Critical Reading: Varga and Holm's Re-examination of the Halden Pilot

The first half of this comment is strong. Using the microdata, it confirms with numbers most of the concerns raised about the Halden paper. The second half is weaker: the conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" goes well beyond what the authors' own analysis shows. It also leaves out the one piece of evidence that most directly contradicts it.

## What it does well

- **It puts numbers on the corrections.** Moving from scheduled to actual hours, and from manager ratings to records, takes the per-hour gain from 23.4% to 10.8%. Before, these problems could only be argued in principle.
- **It finds a reporting discrepancy that matters.** The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". According to the microdata, seven withdrew after the schedule began, and six of the nine cited workload or output. If that is right, the working paper misdescribed its own attrition, and Halden should correct it.
- **The manager-rating bias is systematic.** Managers rated output higher than their own records in 19 of 23 organisations. A sign test gives p ≈ 0.001 (two-sided), so this is unlikely to be chance.
- **It is open about its subsets.** The data note acknowledges that the corrected estimates apply to non-random subsets.
- **Its findings agree with independent evidence.** Actual hours fell 14.1%, close to Varden's 13% in case-processing. Two separate sources therefore suggest that a 20% scheduled cut produces roughly a 13–14% real cut.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Records, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Records, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours (27 orgs) | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours (17 orgs) | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 | −2.6% ✓ |

Two figures do not hold up:

**1. The breakdown of hours does not add up.** Section 3 says two things explain why hours fell less than 20%: an extra 0.7 hours per day on the four working days, and 1.6 hours per week logged on the day off. Those would give about 32 + (4 × 0.7) + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Starting from the baseline day of 8.06 hours makes the gap larger, not smaller. To reach 34.6, the extra time per working day would have to be about 0.25 hours. One of these figures is probably wrong, or the extra 0.7 per day is measured against something unstated.

**2. The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated.** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD between months three and six, about 0.107 SD per month. At that rate it reaches zero about 2.7 months later, around **month 9**, not month 10. The difference is small, but extrapolating a line through just two points is fragile in any case (see below).

## Issues

### 1. The abstract claims more correction than the analysis performs

According to the abstract, correcting "the first three" problems (attrition, output and hours) brings the gain down to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never quantified.

A bounding exercise was needed and would have been easy. For example, suppose the nine withdrawn organisations had no per-hour gain at all. Weighting by organisation, the 10.8% would then fall to roughly 9–10%. Even under quite pessimistic assumptions about the dropouts, attrition does not seem able to remove the residual on its own. The comment argues that it does without ever showing it.

### 2. "Entirely an artifact" does not follow from the analysis

The comment's own best estimate, after its corrections, is a **gain of +10.8%**. To call this "entirely" artifact, it needs attrition and novelty to account for the rest. It quantifies neither:

- **Attrition:** not estimated (see above).
- **Novelty:** the argument rests on a straight line through two self-reported energy readings. Energy is not output, and the comment shows no link between the two. Output per hour may not have tracked energy at all. The two readings also show energy rising and then falling, so a straight line is an assumption, not something the data show.

Demonstrating that biases exist does not demonstrate that they explain the whole effect. A conclusion the evidence supports would be closer to: "the corrected gain is about 11% in a non-random subset of survivors, and attrition and novelty could reduce it further by unknown amounts."

### 3. It leaves out the Varden result that contradicts it

The comment calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions Varden's **case-processing stratum**. That stratum addresses every problem the comment raises:

- **Selection:** offices were randomised, so there was no self-selection, and no attrition is reported.
- **Output measure:** output came from administrative records, not manager ratings.
- **Hours:** actual hours came from timesheets, including claimed overtime.
- **Comparison:** there was a concurrent control group.
- **Duration:** nine months, longer than Halden's six.

Under all those conditions, it found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI 6.9 to 18.4)**. That is almost identical to the comment's corrected Halden figure of 10.8%. The match suggests the residual reflects something real rather than measurement artefacts.

Novelty is the only explanation Varden cannot rule out. Even there, the control staff also knew a trial was running, which partly offsets a pure Hawthorne effect.

The comment's use of the counter stratum is also selective. It cites the fall in output per employee there, but not the **+6.7%** gain in output per actual hour in the same stratum. That gain is better explained by queueing, since busier staff handle more contacts per hour, but omitting it still misrepresents the evidence.

### 4. It applies its burden of proof unevenly

The comment dismisses the meetings hypothesis as a "post hoc account" built on seven data points. It then accepts a novelty hypothesis built on two data points of a different variable. Both explanations are speculative. Holding one to a strict standard while relying on the other is inconsistent.

The meetings critique also argues against a stronger claim than Varden made. Varden's authors called the analysis unregistered and exploratory. They said seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism", and they registered a confirmatory test. The comment's warning that the result "should not be cited as a mechanism" is something Varden's authors already said themselves.

The phrase "selected for analysis after the results were known" may also be inaccurate. Varden says the meetings data were collected in month six at managers' request, which was before the nine-month results existed.

Finally, the meetings explanation does not support the "artifact" conclusion. If cutting meetings raises output per hour, that is a real gain, not a measurement error.

### 5. Smaller points

- **"A change that staff chose":** in Halden, participation was voluntary at the organisation level, and all staff in participating units moved to the new schedule. Individual staff did not choose.
- **No confidence intervals.** None of the corrected estimates in Table 2, and neither the −3.8-point output gap nor the −11.2% retail figure, comes with an interval. The 17-organisation estimate in particular could have wide uncertainty.
- **The retail figure rests on three organisations.** It points the same way as the other evidence, but it is too thin to carry much weight on its own.
- **Revenue:** the real-terms correction is right and useful. Using general consumer prices to deflate revenue is a rough approach, since prices in each sector may have moved differently, but the conclusion still holds.

## How the three studies fit together

| | Halden (as reported) | Halden (Varga & Holm corrected) | Varden case-processing | Varden counter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Actual hours change | assumed −20% | −14% | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | (+23.4% scheduled) | +10.8% | +12.5% | +6.7% (queueing) |
| Output per employee | −1.3% (manager) | −4.6% (records) | −2.1% | −11.4% |
| Control group | no | no | yes | yes |

Taken together, the corrected observational estimate and the randomised estimate for office-type work both land at roughly **+11–12% per actual hour**. Output per employee falls slightly, between 2% and 5%. Two very different designs agreeing like this is the strongest evidence in the set. It points to a real but modest per-hour gain in work that does not depend on staff being present. Its durability past nine months is unproven.

## Fair summary

The comment correctly shows that Halden's headline gain was more than doubled by two things: counting scheduled rather than actual hours, and relying on manager ratings rather than records. It also shows that attrition was misreported and probably biased the results upward, and that revenue fell in real terms.

Its corrected estimate is an output-per-hour gain of about 11% among surviving organisations with usable data. That estimate is close to the randomised Varden estimate for comparable work.

The further claim that the whole gain is artifact is not supported. Attrition and novelty are asserted rather than quantified, the novelty argument rests on two self-reported data points, and the randomised evidence that contradicts the claim is left out.
